content: Childhood tuberculosis (TB) is a significant yet often overlooked global public health issue. Treatment with rifampicin-containing anti-TB drugs administered daily for six months has been shown to cure over 90% of infected children. However, poor adherence to this daily regimen can compromise treatment success. Intermittent regimens, where medications are given two or three times a week under direct observation, have been associated with better adherence in observational studies. Despite this, it remains unclear how intermittent regimens compare to daily treatment in terms of cure rates. Current international and national guidelines differ on whether intermittent regimens should be used for treating TB in children. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of intermittent short-course anti-TB regimens (administered twice or thrice weekly) compared to daily short-course regimens in children with TB. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, up to May 30, 2013. Experts were also contacted to identify relevant published, unpublished, and ongoing trials. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving children aged 15 years or younger diagnosed with TB, based on World Health Organization (WHO) diagnostic categories 1, 2, or 3. All treatment regimens included rifampicin for at least the first two months. The review authors independently screened and selected trials, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. Clarifications were sought from trial authors when necessary. Relative risks with 95% confidence intervals were pooled, and a random-effects model was used in cases of significant heterogeneity. The overall quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Four trials, published between 1996 and 2000, were included in the review. These trials randomized 563 children (465 evaluable participants) aged five months to 15 years to receive either intermittent twice-weekly or daily anti-TB treatment. Two trials were conducted in India, one in South Africa, and one in Turkey. All trials used rifampicin and isoniazid, three included pyrazinamide, and one included streptomycin. The drug combinations and treatment durations varied between trials, and none of the trials used regimens currently recommended for childhood TB. Additionally, none of the trials reported whether any of the children were HIV-positive. When comparing twice-weekly intermittent regimens to daily regimens, the trials did not detect significant differences in the number of patients cured. However, the trials were small, and the comparator regimens were not standardized. The evidence quality was rated as very low. The trials were also underpowered to provide reliable estimates for outcomes such as death, relapse, and treatment-limiting adverse events. Reported adherence to treatment was similar between the two groups (87% for intermittent regimens versus 84% for daily regimens), but the evidence quality was again very low. No trials were identified that compared the commonly used thrice-weekly intermittent regimen to the daily regimen. In conclusion, the available trials are insufficient to either support or refute the use of intermittent twiceor thrice-weekly short-course regimens over daily short-course regimens for treating TB in children. Further randomized trials conducted in high TB-transmission settings are needed to guide policy and clinical practice.
